title: The Divinity of Christ and the Earthen Vessels of Apostles
english: …to our hearts, toward the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

The mystagogue clarifies through the present word that faith is directed toward God, even if it were practiced in the face of Christ; for both Jews and Greeks have been called toward the experiential knowledge of Christ—the former as if from error and false worship toward the true knowledge of God, and the latter toward a more precise knowledge, being tutored by the Law.
Such is also the law-giving Paul, who is seen as having been slightly cautioned in comparison to those instructed in the lessons of the Law, because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ.

When, therefore, the mystagogues preach Christ, and those believing in God believe in the one and true God, how can Christ not be God? He is no bastard, no pseudonym, and certainly not a stranger to the Father, but rather truly is from Him according to His nature.
For the mind of those who wander has been reproached by an irrational and demonic deception, but God promised that the light would shine up upon us out of the darkness.
For he once said through the voice of Isaiah, "The people sitting in darkness, behold a great light; those dwelling in a land and shadow of death, light shall shine upon you" (Isaiah 9:2).

And the law-giving David says, speaking from the face of those in gloom and darkness, "That you light my lamp, Lord; you God, my God, you light my darkness" (Psalm 18:28). Since, therefore, the promise of the Father has been fulfilled for us, and the divine, intelligible light has dawned upon us, we have known His glory in the face of Christ.

Furthermore, if Christ is truly God by nature, have we not seen the glory of the Father in him? For even as we clearly hear God and the Father saying, 'My glory to another I will not give;' behold, He has given it to the Son.

Therefore, the Son is not another from Him, except insofar in subsistence and His own personal existence, so that the Father might not appear to have lied to the person of the Son by setting forth His own glory; and so that God is known to be in Him by nature and through Him.
For He is indeed a person, an icon, and a radiance of His subsistence; and the Son is revealed by the Father, and He Himself also reveals the Father to us within Himself.
In earthen vessels.

The term 'earthen vessels' refers to the common; for our tradition of the divine mysteries is not delivered to us in a pomp of words, but in a language accustomed to all, so that everyone might learn and understand.

What then, O Paul? For it was not possible for God, who makes all things wise, to make the holy apostles so extremely eloquent that they might easily, and even more than those being struck by the blow of words, amaze those who encounter them; yes, he says, for He Himself is the provider of wisdom.
But in earthen vessels—that is, in a small possession—He has locked up a treasure for us.
Through what reason? So that the excess of the power might be of God and not from ourselves.
In this way, He persuaded all to run toward the faith.
For if the word had been brilliant within them, it would have seemed that the faith of those called had not become an upright standing by His own power.
Since no one can be persuaded by bare words alone that he has become a partaker of God through the superabundance of this power.

We call ourselves pottery vessels, for we are bodies surrounded by perceptible things, thinking with such a mind; since we are still surrounded by the flesh, which hinders the vision of the truth, we possess knowledge concerning the Trinity, the excess of the greatness of this knowledge is not from us, but is made known to us by the power of God existing within us.
In all things they are afflicted, but not distressed (2 Cor 4:8)...
For they appear to have triumphed over death by their piety toward Him and by drawing from Him.
Yet even if they have had to suffer this, they nonetheless live, for they are destined to live with God.
And as the word of wisdom says, 'It seemed in the eyes of men' (Job 29:7)...

title: Mortification and Life in Christ
english: They are reckoned as having died, and their going forth was counted as evil treatment; our departure from them is utter destruction. But they are in peace, and their hope of immortality is full. What, then, is the meaning of their labors? Paul again interprets, saying: We always carry about in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus too may be made evident in our mortal flesh.

We affirm there are two ways of understanding this mortification spoken of here: one is intellectual and spiritual, the other is apprehended through bodily sensation. For God, who exists and has come forth from God according to nature, his Only-begotten Word, prepared for himself a body from the earth; he took upon himself this mortal, human frame, endowed with a rational soul. His purpose was to mortify sin in the flesh and to still the impulse of its innate movements that draw us toward outward pleasures.

Yet the Word, being God, did not establish this for his own sake, but that he might see and endure the sufferings beyond those within us. Indeed, he knows no sin. Rather, he has transmuted within himself the entirety of human nature into a holy and blameless life, when he became man and appeared in the form that is with us. Thus he came to hold first place in all things, so that we, following in his steps, might possess within ourselves his mortification — that is, the powerlessness of sin's strength in our flesh — and thereby be empowered to embrace both this mortification and the blameless life into eternal being.

He became obedient to God and Father, as Scripture says, even to the point of death, laying down his life for the sheep. He died once for sin—meaning for the sin of the world—having made propitiation through faith. The one who lives, lives to God. Therefore, the mystagogues carry in their own bodies this mortification, earned through sufferings and continuing even to his death, so that the life of Jesus, as he himself declared, may be revealed in our bodies.

They too shall live to God, living the holy, blameless, and blessed life. He especially remembers this mortification and yet life, for even now the minds of those who came before, tested by trials and hardships which they willingly endured to fulfill the apostles’ glorious course, bear witness. Nor does he in any way less urge us to think thus, solely and interpreting to them what he said.

For he immediately adds: We who live are continually delivered to death through Jesus, so that through these things he shows they willingly endure the death of the flesh, out of piety toward Christ. Their aim is not to gaze upon present things, but to anticipate the future and the rewards of the 347 labors. They make no account of those who sweat from the struggles, but rather seek the heavenly goods, reasoning about the breadth of God’s ambition. Therefore they are delivered to death through Jesus so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in mortal flesh.
What is the life of Jesus? It is incorruptibility and sanctification, great glory and heavenly in nature.

For it will be revealed to us in due seasons when the judge descends from heaven above, and he will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working of his power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.
Thus the death is at work in us, but the life is in you.
For they imitate their own lord, the mystagogues of what is under the sun, and they have set their own souls, that we who once wandered might gain the life from the faith which is into Christ.
Therefore, we who once wandered might gain the life from the faith which is into Christ.

title: The Inward Renewal Amid Outward Suffering
english: They say through the voice of the one who sings as to the Lord our Jesus Christ, 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter' (Romans 8:36).
Therefore, we do not lose heart, but even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).

It is fitting to approach the thought of these matters without harshness, as is common to all who have chosen godliness, having set before them the goal, for the flesh indeed wages war against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, as it is written (Galatians 5:17).
These things are opposed to one another.
And so we say that every kind of necessity, when the flesh is in some measure corrupted and its motions enfeebled, then the other—namely, the mindset of the Spirit—grows all the more vigorously.
He brings in a recounting of causes and, as it were, a recollection of what was previously said, introducing the 'Therefore'.

He then said: 'Indeed, if we who are alive are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made visible in our hearts, and we possess this hope, he says—yes, even to those who are about to come and attain to it—we do not lose heart, for we foresee the beauty of the glory to come; but even if affliction should come upon us, we endure it nobly.'
For if indeed, as mere humans, we suffer pain and endure some bodily harm, yet we are not overcome by these things.
For the inward person of us is being renewed.
And the message is common to all.
Therefore, when to those engaged in the labors of training our outward self is being corrupted, then necessarily our inward self is renewed day by day.

And furthermore, upon the things that have been said, since to Jews and also to Greeks we proclaimed Jesus, they have endured terrible and unbearable persecutions, and their bodies have been worn down by the labors they undertook.
Yet the greater the labor, the more I think it would reasonably follow that the opposition against grace should be met with an even greater supply of divine favor.
For our present, light affliction is working for us an excess upon excess—an eternal weight of glory—while we do not fix our gaze on what is seen, but on what is unseen (2 Corinthians 4:17-18).
For the things seen are temporary, but the things unseen are eternal.

He strengthens those who wish to contend: making the contests seem small, yet lifting up the crowns for the victors; placing the light burden upon our afflictions, but the weighty glory upon the reward.

For those who make measured progress in this life on account of what is temporary, even if it should abound to excess, still they look forward to passing into an eternal weight of glory, because the good things of the age to come surpass mere speech.
Therefore, we must not fix our attention on the seen, temporary things, but on the unseen, eternal ones.
We know that if our earthly tent—the body—is torn down, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (Job 4:19).

For it is written: 'Those who dwell in houses of clay, from the same clay we are.', thus we understand that when death has destroyed our earthly tent, that is our body, it will not be long—according to the evident time of the resurrection—before we receive a heavenly dwelling, that is, immortality itself.
He declares that this dwelling is from above, first of all because the thing needed is God-given.

Moreover, by this very reason, since all those who dwell above in the city—I mean the orders of the holy angels—exist in incorruptible and imperishable bodies, the angelic nature has been released from this earthly thickness.
Therefore, the building from God, the house not made by hands and moreover eternal, he names incorruptibility.
And indeed in this we groan, desiring to put on our dwelling from heaven.
Therefore, we groan as being weighed down by corruption, yet we cling to the things above.
